Israeli Elections - 4/4
Here's the lingering question that a lot of people are asking. If the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot reaches 61 seats, what fundamentally changes, if anything?
More than nothing, but not a whole lot!
On Gaza: Nothing is going to fundamentally change. Both blocs will maintain the IDF presence in Gaza. Neither bloc is interested in ending the genocide. Eisenkot’s main beef with Netanyahu was quibbling over rescuing hostages and propping up Hamas to undermine the Palestinian Authority.
A Palestinian State: No matter who wins, Palestinians lose. Statehood is not on the table for either bloc. The main difference with an Eisenkot government would be the same ugly apartheid conditions with better PR discipline.
Iran, Lebanon, Syria: No difference whatsoever. Eisenkot is salty about competently conducting the wars. He is still in favor of them. He just wants higher-quality violence.
The West Bank: This is the one big split between the two major blocs. Netanyahu is in the process of total annexation of the West Bank. He gave the psychopath Itamar Ben Gvir control of the police and he has allowed Smotrich’s settler gangs to run wild. Eisenkot has publicly stated he will bring the area back under military command, bring back administrative detention for violent settlers, demolish their illegal outposts, etc. Basically he is promising to initiate a crackdown on the settler gangs, in theory.
Netanyahu himself: He is currently on trial for bribery, probably guilty. This would be another important change. Netanyahu has used the powers of the state to shield himself from prosecution. So maybe he’ll go to prison this time? Who knows.
October 7th: Eisenkot is promising to create a state commission with subpoena power to investigate the entire event and everything that preceded it. This commission has been consistently blocked by Netanyahu. Needless to say, he’s hiding something. So, maybe we find out he let it happen on purpose. Or maybe nothing happens.
The draft: Eisenkot would draft the Haredim and there would be a temper tantrum of monumental proportions. This is mostly just for the slapstick comedy we'll get from watching the Israelis fight amongst themselves.
In short: Apartheid with better optics or genocidal pogroms with zero fucks given. These are the choices.

💵 Lockheed Martin bags $694M contract to build hypersonic missile - report
Despite a record of failed flight tests that nearly killed the program in 2023, the US Air Force has awarded Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract to move the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW) beyond prototyping and into production, Stars and Stripes reports.
With a range of 1,000 miles and speeds exceeding Mach 5, the boost-glide missile destroys its target on impact using kinetic energy. Testing has mainly involved the B-52H, with the B-1B also slated for future use. The deal was signed on September 29 under the Pentagon’s Enterprise-Wide Agile Acquisition Contract model — a fast-track mechanism that bypasses the usual oversight.
Even with the new contract in hand, the Pentagon has not disclosed how many missiles it will buy or when they will enter service — leaving Washington’s long-running hypersonic ambitions facing another test: turning years of development and spending into a deployable weapon.
In October, the US Army confirmed that the country is running more than three years behind schedule in fielding its first hypersonic weapons system, Dark Eagle. Lockheed has burned through billions of dollars on programs that repeatedly miss their deadlines — while the Pentagon keeps writing the checks.

events.text:
🇮🇷💰 Iran Gives Old Batteries Graphene Upgrade to Cut Imports
Iranian manufacturer Platin Iran has started selling graphene-enhanced lead-acid batteries, claiming over 60% more capacity and potentially 50% lower lifetime operating costs. For a technology dating back to the 19th century, that's a fairly ambitious second act.
Instead of reinventing the battery, Iranian researchers added a three-dimensional form of graphene to its electrodes. That helps electricity flow and aims to slow the corrosion and chemical buildup that wear ordinary batteries out.
That matters for the unglamorous machinery keeping modern life running, from cell towers to data centers and power plants. When the electricity goes out, backup batteries keep communications and essential controls working. Nobody wants to discover the weak link during a blackout.
Platin Iran says the new design cuts hydrogen gas release by at least 10% and reduces corrosion. In June, the company reported roughly double the charge-discharge cycle life of ordinary batteries, although buyers would pay about 30% more upfront. The idea is to recover that premium through fewer replacements.
October's figures put the capacity gain above 60% and the increase in service life at no less than 10%. Those are different measures, and a longer life in laboratory cycling doesn't guarantee the same result in everyday standby use. The 50% savings estimate still needs proof at scale.
The project began in 2021 with researchers from Amirkabir University of Technology and the Institute for Color Science and Technology. It has since reached industrial production, with two units sold, including one to the Tabriz Gas Transmission Company. It's an early commercial foothold, rather than a mass rollout.
Iran also has an import bill to tackle, with Platin Iran estimating that comparable batteries worth roughly $4M enter the country each year. Replacing even part of that demand with domestic production would give operators another source of equipment and reduce dependence on overseas suppliers.
There may be flashier ways to advertise a technological breakthrough, but improving a battery already used across industry has its advantages. If the promised durability survives real-world testing, Iran could turn a familiar piece of backup equipment into a modest but useful win for its industrial independence.
